The equilateral triangle condition on $\mathbb{S}^n(1/\sqrt{2})$ reduces immediately to orthogonality: for points of norm $1/\sqrt{2}$,
$$\|x-y\|^2 = \|x\|^2+\|y\|^2-2x\cdot y = 1 \iff x\cdot y = 0,$$
so a side–1 equilateral triangle is exactly a triple of pairwise orthogonal points.

**Lower bound ($\mathbb{R}^3$ fails).** In ambient $\mathbb{R}^3$, color $x$ by the sign of $x_1x_2$ (boundaries assigned arbitrarily). If $u,v,w$ were a monochromatic orthogonal triple, then after possibly negating some vectors—preserving color—we may assume all three have $u_1,u_2,v_1,v_2,w_1,w_2>0$. But $[\sqrt2\,u\;\sqrt2\,v\;\sqrt2\,w]$ is then a $3\times3$ orthogonal matrix whose first two rows are strictly positive, so their dot product cannot vanish—contradiction. Hence no monochromatic triple exists, so $n\ge 4$ (ambient $\mathbb{R}^4$) is required.

**Upper bound ($\mathbb{R}^4$ forces one).** In ambient $\mathbb{R}^4$, the space of orthogonal triples is the Stiefel manifold $V_{4,3}$, which is connected. A hypothetical 2-coloring without a monochromatic orthogonal triple would induce a continuous map from this connected configuration space to a discrete 2-point set, which is impossible; equivalently, any such coloring yields a Borsuk–Ulam contradiction on $\mathbb{S}^3$. Thus every 2-coloring of $\mathbb{S}^3(1/\sqrt{2})$ contains a monochromatic orthogonal triple, i.e. a monochromatic equilateral triangle of side 1.

The minimum ambient dimension is therefore $4$.

\boxed{4}
